lead: ES6, also called ES2015, is the 2015 update to JavaScript that gave the language block-scoped names, short arrow functions, class syntax and file modules. Before it, var leaked across blocks and big programs shared one global script file. ES6 keeps each name near where it is used and splits a large app into small files. Modern browsers and Node.js accept it. You use it in every React component, every fetch call and every npm package in later units.
prereq: You need: 3.1, 3.2 and 3.4, because this chapter rewrites their code in ES6.

blocks.text: var is function-scoped: a var name is visible in the whole function, even before its line. let and const are block-scoped: the name lives only inside the nearest { }. A block is any pair of braces, such as an if body, a loop body or a bare { }. This stops a loop counter from leaking into the rest of the function.

let allows reassignment but not re-declaration in the same block. const must be initialized when declared and cannot be reassigned. const does not freeze an object: const o = {}; o.x = 1; is legal, because const binds the name o to one object; the object's properties can still change. Object.freeze(o) stops adding, changing or deleting o's own properties; it is shallow, so objects held inside o can still change.

Both let and const are hoisted to the top of their block but stay in a temporal dead zone (TDZ) until the declaration runs. Reading one before that line throws ReferenceError. var instead reads as undefined. Prefer const by default, let when the value must change, and avoid var in new code.

Template literals use backticks, not quotes: `Hi ${name}`. The ${ } inserts a value and the literal may span lines. Destructuring copies values by pattern: const [a, b] = [1, 2]; and const {name, age} = user;. Rename with {name: n} and give defaults with {age = 18}.
Spread ... expands: [...arr] copies an array, {...obj} copies an object. Rest collects: function f(...args) puts extra arguments in args; const [first, ...rest] = arr puts the tail in rest.

An arrow function is shorter: const add = (a, b) => a + b;. One parameter may drop parentheses. A multi-statement body needs braces and return. An arrow has no own this or arguments; this comes from the enclosing scope. Do not use an arrow as an object method when the method needs the object's this; use a method shorthand or a normal function.

Class syntax groups a constructor and methods. class Animal { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } speak() { return this.name; } static kind() { return 'animal'; } get label() { return this.name.toUpperCase(); } }. constructor runs on new. speak is a method. static kind() belongs to the class, not an instance. get label() is a getter read as a.label. In class Dog extends Animal { constructor(name) { super(name); } speak() { return this.name + ' barks'; } }, extends inherits and super(name) calls the parent constructor.

Modules split code into files. Named export: export const x = 1; export function f() {}; import: import { x, f } from './m.js';. Rename with import { x as y }. Default export: export default class App {}; import: import App from './App.js';. One module per file; many named exports, one default. In a browser, load the file as <script type="module" src="./m.js"></script>. A module has its own scope, runs deferred and is strict. Without type="module", import is a syntax error.

for (const v of arr) loops over values. new Map() stores key-value pairs with set, get, has. new Set() stores unique values. Enhanced object literals shorten code: const o = { x, method() {}, [key]: 1 };. Promises are named here only; their behaviour is in 3.6.

spec.aria: Left: three callbacks all point to one var binding i = 3 and print 3 3 3. Right: each callback points to its own let binding j = 0, 1, 2 and prints 0 1 2. Below: add(2, 3) returns 5.

examples.question: Trace this JavaScript code: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); } What does it print? Rewrite the loop with let and give the new output. Then rewrite function add(a, b) { return a + b; } as an arrow function and evaluate add(2, 3).
steps: var i is one function-scoped binding. The three setTimeout callbacks do not read i during the loop.
The loop stops when i reaches 3. Each callback later reads the same i, so the var loop prints 3, 3, 3 on three lines.
With let j, each iteration creates a fresh j. The callbacks capture 0, 1 and 2, so the let loop prints 0, 1, 2.
Arrow rewrite: const add = (a, b) => a + b;. With a = 2 and b = 3, add returns 2 + 3 = 5.
examples.answer: The var loop prints 3 3 3, the let loop prints 0 1 2, and add(2, 3) returns 5.

traps: Assuming const freezes an object: const o = {}; o.x = 1 works. const blocks reassigning the name, not changing the object; Object.freeze stops changes.
Using an arrow function as an object method: it has no own this, so this.name does not see the object. Use method shorthand when you need the object.
Forgetting that var in a loop with setTimeout gives one shared binding: all callbacks print the final value, not 0, 1, 2.
Writing import/export in a browser script without type="module": the browser treats import as a syntax error.
Reading a let or const name before its declaration throws ReferenceError because of the temporal dead zone; var gives undefined instead.

quiz.q: What does const stop: reassignment of the name, or changes inside the object?
quiz.a: const stops reassignment of the name. It does not stop property changes inside the object; Object.freeze does that.

quiz.q: Why does a var loop with setTimeout print the final value three times?
quiz.a: All callbacks share one function-scoped binding that holds the loop's final value (3 in this example), so they all print that final value.

quiz.q: Rewrite function mul(a, b) { return a * b; } as an arrow function and give mul(4, 5).
quiz.a: const mul = (a, b) => a * b; mul(4, 5) returns 20.

quiz.q: Given const s = {name: 'Asha'}; which lines work: s.name = 'Ravi'; s = {}; ?
quiz.a: s.name = 'Ravi' works because the object is mutable. s = {} throws TypeError because const forbids reassigning the name.

quiz.q: Write one named export and its matching import.
quiz.a: export const x = 1; then import { x } from './m.js';

quiz.q: What does adding type="module" to a script tag change?
quiz.a: It makes the browser treat the file as a module: own scope, import/export allowed, deferred execution, strict mode.

quiz.q: Why is an arrow function a bad object method when the method uses this?
quiz.a: An arrow has no own this; it takes this from the enclosing scope, so it does not see the object. Use a method shorthand or a normal function.

quiz.q: What does this print: const m = new Map(); m.set('a', 1); console.log(m.get('a'));

beyond: Not for the exam. ES6 is now the baseline; newer yearly releases add optional chaining, nullish coalescing, top-level await and private class fields. Bundlers such as Vite and webpack use ES modules as their input format and drop unused exports. Search next for 'ES modules browser', 'JavaScript temporal dead zone' and 'class fields JavaScript'.
